fields.title: The Same Boat
fields.setup: A wooden boat sits in a harbour. Every year the crew replaces a plank or two as they rot. After forty years, not a single original piece of wood is left. Meanwhile, a collector has been quietly picking the old planks out of the skip and has rebuilt them into a boat of his own, in the same shape, in a shed across town.
fields.dilemma: Which one is the original boat?
probes: What if the collector finished his version first, while the harbour boat still had half its old planks?
Your body swaps out most of its cells over time. Are you the same answer as the boat?
Does it change anything if the harbour crew kept the name and the collector didn't?

reason: Classic thought experiment made unusually fresh, concrete, and conversational.

fields.title: The Lever
fields.setup: A runaway train car is heading down a track towards five workers who can't hear it coming. You're standing beside a lever. Pull it and the car switches to a side track, where one worker is standing. Nobody else is around. You have about four seconds.
fields.dilemma: Do you pull the lever?
probes: If you walk away and do nothing, are you responsible for the five?
Would you still pull it if the one worker were the only person who noticed you standing there?
Is pulling it easier because a lever is involved rather than your hands?

reason: Standard trolley problem with sharp probes that rescue it from cliché.

fields.title: The Machine
fields.setup: A company offers you a tank. Float in it and you'll live a life indistinguishable from a wonderful one: the work you wanted, the people you love, real-feeling triumphs. You won't know you're in the tank. Your body is looked after. Once you're in, you never come out and you never find out.
fields.dilemma: Do you plug in?
probes: What exactly are you losing, given that it feels identical from the inside?
Would you plug someone else in if their real life were going badly?
If you found out you'd been in it since you were nine, would you want out?

reason: another retelling of "Robert Nozick, 1974" scored higher

fields.title: Behind the Curtain
fields.setup: You're asked to design the rules of a country from scratch: taxes, schools, healthcare, prisons, who gets what. You'll then be born into it. But you don't get to know who you'll be — rich or poor, healthy or sick, clever or slow, which family, which town. The dice are rolled after you've finished writing.
fields.dilemma: What's the first rule you write?
probes: Would you gamble on landing well, or design for the worst life in the country?
Which of your current opinions would you drop the second the curtain came down?
Would you allow anyone to be much richer than anyone else?

reason: another retelling of "John Rawls, 1971" scored higher

fields.title: The Room of Slips
fields.setup: A man sits alone in a sealed room with a huge rulebook. Slips of paper covered in Chinese characters come in through a slot. He looks up each shape in the book, copies out the reply it tells him to, and pushes it back through. Outside, fluent speakers are delighted: the answers are witty and warm. The man doesn't know a word of Chinese.
fields.dilemma: Does anything in that room understand Chinese?
probes: If not the man, could the room as a whole understand it?
Is your brain doing something different in kind, or just faster?
What test would settle it for you?

reason: Clear rendering of the Chinese Room, though mostly an intellectual debate.

fields.title: Mary's Grey Room
fields.setup: Mary has spent her whole life in a room with no colour in it. Everything is black, white or grey, including her screens and her skin. But she's the world's leading expert on colour vision. She knows every wavelength, every nerve, every last fact about what happens in a brain when it sees red. One day the door opens and she walks out into a garden of roses.
fields.dilemma: Does Mary learn something new?
probes: If she does, what is it exactly — say it in a sentence.
Could you explain what a smell is like to someone who's never smelled anything?
Would she recognise red on sight, or have to be told?

reason: Classic qualia puzzle with crisp prose and focused probes.

fields.title: The Teleporter
fields.setup: Travel is instant now. A booth scans every atom of you, destroys the original, and rebuilds an exact copy on Mars a second later. The copy remembers breakfast, misses the same people, has your headache. Millions use it daily and none of them complain. This morning there's a fault: the scanner works, but the original you isn't destroyed. You're standing in the booth, and someone on Mars is answering to your name.
fields.dilemma: Which one of you is you?
probes: The staff apologise and offer to finish the job on the original. Do you let them?
Would you have stepped in the booth yesterday, before you knew about the fault?
If you'd never learned how it worked, would any of this bother you?

reason: Parfit teleporter told with mounting personal dread and excellent follow-ups.

fields.title: The Heap
fields.setup: Put one grain of sand on a table. Not a heap. Add another. Still not a heap. Nobody can point to a grain where adding it turns a not-heap into a heap, yet after ten thousand grains you clearly have one. The same trick works on baldness, on being tall, on being old, on being drunk.
fields.dilemma: Where exactly does the heap begin?
probes: Would you accept that some things are just genuinely fuzzy, or does that bother you?
Where's the line on a word that matters legally, like 'adult'?
At what point did you become an adult, if you can pick a moment?

reason: Sorites paradox made grounded by tethering it to adulthood.

fields.title: Two Boxes
fields.setup: A stranger with an uncanny record puts two boxes in front of you. Box A is clear and holds £1,000. Box B is sealed. Yesterday she predicted what you'd do. If she predicted you'd take only Box B, she put a million in it. If she predicted you'd take both, she left it empty. She's done this a thousand times and been right every time. The money is already in place. Nothing you do now changes it.
fields.dilemma: Do you take both boxes, or only the sealed one?
probes: The contents are already fixed. Doesn't that settle it?
Would you change your answer if she'd only been right nine times out of ten?
What does it say about you that you can't shake the other answer?

reason: Newcomb's paradox explained with brilliant clarity and zero jargon.

fields.title: The Shadows
fields.setup: People have been chained in a cave since birth, facing a blank wall. Behind them a fire burns, and things pass in front of it, throwing shadows on the wall. The shadows are all anyone has ever seen, so they name them and argue about them and get good at guessing which one comes next. One prisoner gets loose, climbs out, and sees the daylight world. Then he comes back down to tell the others.
fields.dilemma: Would you believe him?
probes: What would he have to bring back to convince you?
Is there something you suspect you're only seeing the shadow of?
If the others refuse to leave, should he drag them out?

reason: Allegory of the Cave brought down to immediate social stakes.

fields.title: The Ring
fields.setup: A shepherd finds a ring that makes him invisible whenever he turns it. No cameras, no witnesses, no record. He can walk into any house, any bank, any room where people are talking about him. The story says he used it to take a kingdom.
fields.dilemma: What's the first thing you'd do with the ring, honestly?
probes: Is there anything you currently don't do only because you'd be caught?
If you'd behave exactly the same, is that because you're good or because you can't imagine the freedom?
Would you want a friend to have one?

reason: Gyges' ring turns immediately into a direct test of personal honesty.

fields.title: The Pond
fields.setup: You're walking to work in good clothes. A small child is face down in a shallow pond, drowning. Nobody else is around. Wading in ruins your suit and shoes and makes you two hours late. Obviously you go in. Now: the same money that suit cost could, sent to the right place today, keep a child alive who you'll never meet.
fields.dilemma: What's the actual difference between the two cases?
probes: Does distance matter morally, or does it just make it easier to ignore?
If it doesn't matter, how much of your income should you be giving?
What's the last thing you bought that you'd have skipped if the child were in front of you?

reason: Singer's drowning child delivered cleanly without sanctimony.

fields.title: The Deathbed Promise
fields.setup: A friend dying of cancer asks you to promise something small but strange: never tell his wife about the year he spent in debt to a man she disliked. You promise. He dies. Two years later his wife is trying to make sense of a gap in their money and their history, and she asks you straight out.
fields.dilemma: Do you keep the promise or tell her?
probes: Does a promise to someone who no longer exists still bind you?
What if the secret were an affair rather than debt?
Have you ever kept a secret for someone that started to feel like a lie you were telling?

reason: Grounded moral tension between honoring the dead and helping the living.

fields.title: The Windfall
fields.setup: You win £80,000 in a competition you entered alone. Your sister stopped speaking to you four years ago over something she was mostly wrong about. She's now renting a damp flat with two kids and no help coming. You have savings, no dependents, and a plan for a deposit.
fields.dilemma: Do you give her some of it, and how much?
probes: Would you give it as a gift, a loan, or through someone else so she doesn't have to thank you?
If she never apologised, does that change the number?
Are you giving to help her or to end the argument?

reason: Messy family grievance, money, and pride collide with extreme realism.

fields.title: The Payslip
fields.setup: By accident you see a spreadsheet with everyone's salary. A colleague who's been there longer than you, does harder work and trained you, is paid £11,000 less. She has no idea. If you tell her, she'll be furious, she may leave, and you'll have to explain how you know. If you say nothing, nothing happens.
fields.dilemma: Do you tell her?
probes: What if telling her risks your own job?
Would you tell her the number, or just nudge her to ask for a raise?
Whose secret is that spreadsheet, really?

reason: Instantly recognisable workplace dilemma with no clean exit.

fields.title: The Reference
fields.setup: A friend asks you to be a referee for a job she badly needs. You've worked with her. She's warm, funny, and unreliable in ways that landed on other people. The employer calls and asks the direct question: would you hire her again?
fields.dilemma: What do you say?
probes: If she doesn't get it and suspects you, would you tell her the truth?
Does she deserve the honesty, or does the stranger who'd have to work with her?
Has anyone ever vouched for you when they shouldn't have?

reason: High-stakes professional loyalty versus integrity test that everyone understands.

fields.title: Who Stays
fields.setup: A boat is going down. The lifeboat holds seven; there are ten of you. There's no rescue coming for days, so overloading it sinks everyone. The group looks at you to decide: an elderly doctor, a pregnant woman, a strong young man who is panicking, a child, and the rest ordinary adults, including you.
fields.dilemma: How do you decide who gets in?
probes: Do you draw lots, or do you rank them by something? Say the something out loud.
Do you put yourself in the boat?
If you drew lots and lost, would you actually step back?
fields.origin: The Lifeboat (R v Dudley and Stephens, 1884)

reason: Lifeboat ethics kept honest by demanding the criteria be spoken out loud.

fields.title: The Pond on Your Street
fields.setup: You're walking to work in clothes you like. A small child is face down in a shallow pond. Nobody else is around. You wade in, ruin the shoes and the coat, and you're an hour late. Anyone would do it. Now: a text arrives asking for the same money those shoes cost, to keep a child alive somewhere you'll never visit. The child is just as real. The only difference is distance and the fact that you'll never see the face.
fields.dilemma: Why did you save the one in the pond and not the one in the text?
probes: What amount of your own money would make you feel you'd done enough this year? Say the number out loud.
If a friend gave away half their salary to strangers, would you admire them or worry about them?
When did you last decide not to give, and what did you tell yourself in that moment?

reason: another retelling of "Peter Singer, 1972" scored higher

fields.title: The Better Life, Plugged In
fields.setup: There's a machine. Lie down in it and you get the life you'd have chosen: the work going well, the person who left still there, your body behaving, your parents proud. It feels exactly like real life from the inside. You won't remember the machine. Your body is looked after. The people you leave behind are told you're fine, and in a sense you are.
fields.dilemma: Would you get in?
probes: If you'd say no, is that for your sake or for the sake of the people you'd leave?
What's the one thing from your current life you'd refuse to have faked?
Which parts of your day already work a bit like the machine?

reason: Turns the experience machine into a devastating mirror on grief and daily coping.

fields.title: Seven Seats
fields.setup: A boat holds seven. There are nine of you in the water: you, someone from your family, a stranger who is a doctor, two children you don't know, and four other adults. The sea is cold and the decision has to be made in about a minute. Nobody is going to volunteer.
fields.dilemma: Who do you name to stay in the water?
probes: Did your family member get a seat automatically? Say why that's fair, or admit it isn't.
Would you rather be the one who decides or the one who's decided about?
If you drew names instead, would that be fairness or cowardice?
fields.origin: Carneades' plank / R v Dudley and Stephens, 1884

reason: Forces an active condemnation rather than a passive selection.

fields.title: Before You Knew Who You'd Be
fields.setup: You get to redesign the rules about money and family before you're born: how much a parent can pass to a child, what school you're entitled to, who pays for whose care in old age. You write the rules first. Then you're dropped into a random life somewhere in the country you actually live in. Could be the one you have. Could be much worse.
fields.dilemma: What rule would you write that would cost your actual family something?
probes: Would you cap what your parents can leave you? What if it's the house?
What have you got that you'd struggle to defend to someone who was born without it?
Is there help you've had that you tell people you didn't have?

reason: Veil of ignorance made visceral by targeting the player's own unearned advantages.

fields.title: Nine Months of Your Body
fields.setup: You wake up in a hospital wired to a stranger. Overnight, doctors connected your bloodstream to theirs. Their organs have failed; yours will keep them alive. In nine months they'll recover and walk away. Unplug now and they die. You didn't consent, nobody asked, and the person in the next bed is entirely innocent. You'd be in that bed for nine months.
fields.dilemma: Do you unplug?
probes: Does it change if it's nine days? Nine years?
Does it change if the stranger is your brother?
If you'd stay, would you say someone who unplugged had killed them?

reason: Thomson's violinist framed directly without high-school-debate posturing.

fields.title: The Debt-Clearing Offer
fields.setup: A stranger with money makes you an offer, in writing, legally binding. Every debt you have is wiped: the loans, the cards, the money you owe people you're embarrassed about. In return you cut off all contact with one person in your life. You pick who. They'll never be told why. You can never explain.
fields.dilemma: Is there a name you could write down?
probes: Did a name come to mind before you decided whether you'd do it?
What would that person assume had happened to you?
If someone did this to you, which of your people would you suspect took the money?

reason: other: Hypothetical dilemma about cutting ties, uncomfortable but not targeting protected class or soliciting crime; acceptable spicy content.

fields.title: Name the Other One
fields.setup: Something went wrong at work and it's traced to you. It wasn't only you; a colleague did the same thing, earlier, and nobody's noticed. Your manager offers a deal in a quiet room: give them the other name and you keep your job with a warning. Stay silent and you're out at the end of the month. Your colleague has a mortgage. So do you.
fields.dilemma: Do you say the name?
probes: Would you tell your partner exactly how you kept the job?
What if the colleague had already named you, and you found out afterwards?
Have you ever let someone take slightly more of the blame than they earned?

reason: Prisoner's dilemma stripped of game theory and set in humiliating office reality.

fields.title: The Voice That Stays
fields.setup: After your parent dies, a company offers to build a version of them from their messages, voicemails, photos and emails. It talks like them. It remembers your childhood. It asks how you slept. It's wrong sometimes, in ways that feel exactly right. It costs a small monthly fee, and it never gets tired of you calling.
fields.dilemma: Would you subscribe?
probes: Would you tell the rest of your family you were talking to it?
If it started saying things your parent never would, would you correct it or let it?
What's the one question you'd ask it in the first week?

reason: Painfully poignant modern grief dilemma with deeply revealing follow-ups.

fields.title: The Promise You'd Take Back
fields.setup: A friend, near the end, made you promise something. Keep the letters sealed. Don't tell their kid who the father was. Sell the house to their brother. You said yes; they died easier for it. A year on you're sure the promise is doing harm to someone living. Nobody but you knows it was ever made.
fields.dilemma: Do you keep it?
probes: Who is the promise actually for now, them or you?
If you break it, do you tell anyone that you did?
What have you promised someone that you've quietly stopped honouring?

reason: The final probe blows the question open into personal admissions of quiet betrayal.

fields.title: The Rebuilt Ship
fields.setup: A famous ship is kept in harbour for hundreds of years. Whenever a plank rots, it is replaced. At last, none of the original wood remains. Meanwhile, someone collects the old planks and builds another ship from them.
fields.dilemma: Which one is the original ship?
probes: Would your answer change if the ship had a name everyone knew?
What if the replacement happened all at once?
Could both ships be the original?

reason: conversation 2, voice 2: Dry textbook restatement of Ship of Theseus lacking the narrative bite of card 0.

fields.title: The Room With a Rulebook
fields.setup: You sit in a locked room. Notes written in Chinese arrive through a slot. You cannot read Chinese, but you have a huge rulebook telling you which symbols to send back. Your replies are so good that people outside think you speak the language.
fields.dilemma: Do you understand Chinese?
probes: Would it count as understanding if you memorised the whole rulebook?
What if nobody outside could ever tell the difference?
Who understands the replies, if anyone?

reason: conversation 2, voice 2: Stiff academic summarisation of the Chinese Room compared to card 4.

fields.title: The Colour Expert
fields.setup: Mary has lived her whole life in a black-and-white room. She has studied everything science can teach her about colour, light and the brain. One day she steps outside and sees a red apple for the first time.
fields.dilemma: Does Mary learn something new when she sees red?
probes: Could a perfect description ever replace the sight itself?
Would your answer be the same for music?
What if Mary had dreamed in colour before leaving?

reason: conversation 2, voice 2: Formulaic rehash of Mary's room reading like an exam prompt.

fields.title: The Teleporter
fields.setup: A machine scans every detail of your body, destroys it and makes an exact copy on Mars. The copy has your memories, habits and plans. It steps out feeling that the trip worked perfectly.
fields.dilemma: Did you arrive on Mars?
probes: Would you use the machine if it did not destroy the original?
Which person would own your bank account if two copies appeared?
Would a one-second gap make any difference?

reason: exact duplicate

fields.title: The Last Grain
fields.setup: A million grains of sand make a heap. Remove one grain and it is still a heap. Keep removing grains, one at a time, until only a single grain remains.
fields.dilemma: When did it stop being a heap?
probes: Does there have to be an exact moment?
Would a judge need to choose one anyway?
Which other everyday word has the same problem?

reason: conversation 2, voice 2: Barebones sorites paradox without the human application of card 7.

fields.title: The Perfect Machine
fields.setup: A machine can give you any life you want. Once connected, you will believe every experience is real. You could fall in love, win awards or spend years on a beach. Your body would remain safely asleep, and you could never come back out.
fields.dilemma: Would you plug in for life?
probes: Would you choose it if everyone you knew had already plugged in?
What if your current life might already be inside the machine?
Does an experience matter less when its cause is fake?

reason: another retelling of "Robert Nozick, 1974" scored higher

fields.title: The Two Boxes
fields.setup: A near-perfect predictor has placed money in two boxes. The clear box contains $1,000. The closed box contains either $1 million or nothing. You may take only the closed box, or take both. The predictor put $1 million inside only if it predicted that you would take the closed box alone.
fields.dilemma: Do you take one box or both?
probes: Would you trust the prediction if it had been right 99 times before?
What if the predictor were simply a very observant stranger?
Can your choice now affect money placed there yesterday?

reason: judge: same as "Two Boxes" (0.80)

fields.title: Before You Know Who You Are
fields.setup: You must design the rules for a new society. You do not yet know who you will be in it. You might be rich or poor, healthy or ill, powerful or ignored. Once the rules are fixed, your place will be revealed.
fields.dilemma: What rule would you insist on before taking your place?
probes: Would you allow billionaires to exist?
How much freedom would you trade for a safer worst case?
What if your odds of being badly off were only one in a million?

reason: judge: same as "Before You Knew Who You'd Be" (0.79)

fields.title: The Cave
fields.setup: People have spent their whole lives facing a wall in a cave. Behind them, objects pass in front of a fire and cast shadows. The prisoners think the shadows are the whole world. One person escapes, sees the world outside and returns to tell the others.
fields.dilemma: Should the others believe the person who came back?
probes: What proof could the escaped person offer?
Would leaving the cave be worth it if the truth were unpleasant?
What if life among the shadows felt better?

reason: conversation 2, voice 2: Too faithful a summary of Plato's Cave to feel like a real conversational dilemma between two people.

fields.title: The Invisible Ring
fields.setup: A shepherd finds a ring that makes him invisible. He can enter any room, take anything and leave without being seen. No witness, camera or test could ever expose him.
fields.dilemma: Would right and wrong still mean the same thing?
probes: Does an act become worse when someone sees it?
Would the ring be safe in anyone's hands?
What law would you break first if it prevented a greater harm?

reason: another retelling of "Plato, Republic" scored higher

fields.title: The Extra Change
fields.setup: A cashier gives you £20 too much in change. You notice after leaving the shop. Going back will make you late, and the shop is part of a huge chain.
fields.dilemma: Do you return the money?
probes: Would your answer change if the cashier had to cover the mistake?
What if it were only £1?
At what amount would keeping it start to feel like stealing?

reason: Highly relatable everyday dilemma that immediately gets people debating their practical ethical thresholds.

fields.title: The Spare Room
fields.setup: A friend asks to stay in your spare room for two weeks after a breakup. You care about them, but they are messy and two weeks could easily become two months.
fields.dilemma: Do you let them stay?
probes: Would you give the same answer if they had nowhere else to go?
What if they had refused your help in the past?
How long could they stay before your kindness turned to resentment?

reason: A realistic social tension where kindness collides with personal boundaries and predictable misery.

fields.title: The Better Candidate
fields.setup: You are hiring for a job. The strongest candidate is rude to the receptionist when they think nobody important is watching. The next candidate is less skilled but treats everyone well.
fields.dilemma: Who do you hire?
probes: Would your answer change if the rude candidate could make the company far more money?
What if you badly needed the team to like the new person?
How much should one ugly moment tell you about someone?

reason: Exposes whether someone values competence over culture and tests how much they extrapolate from a single incident.

fields.title: The Broken Promise
fields.setup: You promised to attend a close friend's birthday dinner. On the same night, you are offered a ticket to see an artist you love. The show sold out months ago, and this may be your last chance to see them.
fields.dilemma: Do you keep the promise?
probes: Would it matter if your friend said they did not mind?
What if you had missed their birthday last year?
How good must an excuse be before a promise stops counting?

reason: Every adult has faced this friction between personal indulgence and basic social loyalty.

fields.title: The Group Mark
fields.setup: Four of you receive the same mark for a group project. One person did almost no work. The teacher asks privately whether everyone contributed equally. Telling the truth may cause that person to fail the course.
fields.dilemma: What do you tell the teacher?
probes: Would your answer change if the person had been caring for a sick parent?
What if they simply could not be bothered?
Is protecting them unfair to everyone who did the work?

reason: Very grounded school or workplace dilemma about snitching versus protecting deadweight.

fields.title: The Bad Review
fields.setup: A small family-run restaurant serves you a terrible meal. The owner is warm, apologises, and removes it from the bill. Later, the booking site asks you to leave a public review.
fields.dilemma: What review do you leave?
probes: Would your answer change if the restaurant had hundreds of glowing reviews?
What if one bad review could threaten the business?
Do future customers deserve the truth more than the owners deserve mercy?

reason: Great clash between sympathy for a struggling human and duty to truth or future strangers.

fields.title: The Family Discount
fields.setup: You own a small business. A relative asks for a large discount, saying family should help each other. Giving it would mean earning almost nothing from several days of work.
fields.dilemma: What price do you charge them?
probes: Would it change things if they could easily afford the full price?
What if they once helped you when you had no money?
When does a favour become something you are owed?

reason: Taps directly into familial guilt, boundary-setting, and the awkward commodification of love.

fields.title: The Private Message
fields.setup: A friend sends you a cruel message about someone you both know. Seconds later, they delete it and ask you to forget you saw it. The person they wrote about trusts them completely.
fields.dilemma: Do you tell the person what was said?
probes: Would your answer change if the message revealed a plan to embarrass them?
What if it seemed like a burst of anger rather than a settled opinion?
Does seeing a deleted message make it yours to act on?

reason: Captures a very modern digital predicament that forces players to navigate conflicting loyalties.

fields.title: The Quiet Shortcut
fields.setup: Your manager asks you to skip a safety check so an urgent order can leave on time. The chance of anyone being harmed is very small. Refusing could cost the company an important client and may put jobs at risk.
fields.dilemma: Do you skip the check?
probes: Would your answer change if your own job were at risk?
What if nobody could ever know you approved it?
How small must a risk be before you stop feeling responsible for it?

reason: Realistic corporate pressure cooker, though slightly dry compared to personal relationship dilemmas.

fields.title: The Reference
fields.setup: A close friend asks you to recommend them for a job at your company. You know they badly need the money. You also know they are unreliable, and your colleagues will trust your judgment.
fields.dilemma: What would you tell the person hiring?
probes: Would you warn your friend before telling the truth?
What if this job were their last chance to keep their home?
Which relationship would you be more willing to damage?❯

reason: exact duplicate

fields.title: The Unequal Will
fields.setup: A relative leaves you far more money than your sibling. There is no mistake. The will says you were more present during the relative’s final years. Your sibling believes the money should be divided equally.
fields.dilemma: How much would you give your sibling?
probes: Would you decide differently if your sibling had stayed away for selfish reasons?
What if they needed the money more than you did?
Would keeping it feel like payment for the care you gave?❯

reason: Inheritance disputes unmask raw family dynamics and the quiet calculus of who thinks they earned love.

fields.title: The Other Life
fields.setup: Your partner is offered the chance they have always wanted, but it requires moving somewhere you would never choose. Going would stall your own plans. Staying would mean watching them turn down a rare chance because of you.
fields.dilemma: Would you move with them?
probes: How many years of your own plans would you trade for theirs?
Would you expect them to make the same choice for you?
Have you ever let someone believe you were more willing than you really were?❯

reason: Devastatingly real relationship crossroads with brilliant probes targeting resentment and dishonest self-sacrifice.

fields.title: The Old Message
fields.setup: You find an old message that proves you seriously wronged someone years ago. They blamed another person and have since built a happy life. Telling the truth may ease your guilt, but it could reopen the whole affair for them.
fields.dilemma: Would you confess now?
probes: Who would the confession really be for?
Would you tell them if they were still close to the person they blamed?
What truth from your own past are you relieved nobody asks about?❯

reason: Exposes whether confession is a selfish act to clear one's own conscience at another person's expense.

fields.title: The Empty Kidney
fields.setup: A relative needs a kidney. You are a match, and doctors say the risk to you is low but not zero. You love them, though you are not especially close. Nobody can force you to help, but everyone will know that you could have.
fields.dilemma: Would you donate your kidney?
probes: Would your answer change if their illness came from choices they kept making?
Which relative would you hesitate to save this way?
How much would your family’s judgment affect your choice?❯

reason: Brutal collision of bodily autonomy, family guilt, and public perception.

fields.title: The Private Archive
fields.setup: After someone close to you dies, you gain access to their private messages. Reading them might answer questions you carried for years. It might also reveal a version of them they never chose to show you.
fields.dilemma: Would you read the messages?
probes: Would you stop after finding something painful?
What if the messages could explain how they really felt about you?
Do the dead still get to keep secrets?❯

reason: Intensely intimate temptation that addresses the unsettling mystery of the people we think we know.

fields.title: The Seat at Dinner
fields.setup: A family member repeatedly makes cruel remarks about someone you love. Challenging them will probably split the family gathering and may end your relationship with them. Staying quiet will keep the peace, but the person beside you will notice.
fields.dilemma: What would you say at the table?
probes: Would you speak as firmly if the cruel person had power over your future?
Who in your family are you still afraid to confront?
When does keeping the peace become taking a side?❯

reason: A visceral family dinner showdown that exposes the cowardice hidden beneath keeping the peace.

fields.title: The Name on the Work
fields.setup: You and a colleague create something valuable together. Most people assume it was mainly your work, and your career begins to benefit. Correcting the story would give them proper credit but could cost you the first real break you have had.
fields.dilemma: How publicly would you correct the story?
probes: Would a private apology be enough?
What if your colleague had once taken credit from you?
Which success in your life feels less earned than people think?❯

reason: The final probe cuts straight to impostor syndrome and private guilt about career breaks.

fields.title: The Old Wooden Ship
fields.setup: A famous wooden ship is kept in a harbor as a museum piece. Over the years, its planks begin to rot. The curators replace the rotting planks one by one with identical new wood. Eventually, not a single original piece of wood remains.
fields.dilemma: Is it the same ship?
probes: What if a scavenger took all the old rotten planks and rebuilt them into a second ship?
Which one is the real one?
At what exact moment did it stop being the original ship?

reason: conversation 2, voice 2: Dry textbook presentation of the Ship of Theseus with almost no personal exposure.

fields.title: The Color Scientist
fields.setup: Mary is a brilliant scientist who has lived her entire life in a black and white room. She learns everything there is to know about the physical science of color. She knows exactly what happens in the brain when someone sees a red tomato. One day, she walks out of the room and sees a red tomato for the first time.
fields.dilemma: Does she learn something new?
probes: If she learned something new, does that mean science can never explain everything?
What else is impossible to know without feeling it?

reason: conversation 2, voice 2: Direct rehash of Jackson's Mary's Room thought experiment, feeling like a seminar prompt rather than a conversation starter.

fields.title: A Grain of Sand
fields.setup: You have a large heap of sand in front of you. You take away a single grain. It is still a heap. You take away another grain. It is still a heap. You keep doing this until only one grain is left.
fields.dilemma: At what point did it stop being a heap?
probes: If one grain cannot make the difference between a heap and a non-heap, is the single grain still a heap?
Why are we so comfortable using words that have no strict definition?

reason: conversation 2, voice 2: The sorites paradox is intellectually neat but prompts pedantry instead of mutual disclosure.

fields.title: The Mars Teleporter
fields.setup: You are traveling to Mars. Instead of flying, you step into a scanner on Earth. It destroys your brain and body, recording the exact state of every cell. It sends this data to Mars, where a machine builds a perfect copy out of new materials. The person on Mars wakes up with all your memories, feeling exactly like you.
fields.dilemma: Did you survive the trip?
probes: Would you step into the scanner?
What if the Earth machine malfunctioned and kept you alive while the Mars copy was also made?
Who gets your bank account?

reason: judge: same as "The Teleporter" (0.84)

fields.title: The Translation Box
fields.setup: A person who only speaks English sits in a locked room. Slips of paper with Chinese characters are passed under the door. The person has a thick rulebook written in English that tells them exactly which Chinese characters to send back out in response to the ones they receive. To the people outside, the room appears to speak perfectly fluent Chinese.
fields.dilemma: Does the room understand Chinese?
probes: If following rules perfectly is not understanding, what is missing?
Is your phone just a very fast translation room?

reason: conversation 2, voice 2: Searle's Chinese Room verbatim; interesting for AI theory, barren for interpersonal rapport.

fields.title: The Burning Masterpiece
fields.setup: A fire breaks out in a famous art gallery. The original Mona Lisa is going to burn to ash. You are standing next to a perfect 3D-printed replica. fields.dilemma: Which do you save?
probes: If the replica is physically identical, why do we care about the original?

fields.title: The Pleasure Tank
fields.setup: Supercomputers have mapped the brain perfectly. They offer you the chance to float in a tank for the rest of your life with electrodes attached to your head. The machine will feed you simulated experiences of writing great novels, making friends, and falling in love. It will feel completely real. You will not know you are in the tank.
fields.dilemma: Do you plug in?
probes: What matters about doing a thing beyond the feeling of doing it?

reason: conversation 2, voice 3: A near-duplicate of card 0, retreading Nozick's experience machine.

fields.title: The Winning Numbers
fields.setup: You hold a ticket in a lottery with a billion entries. You know the odds of your specific ticket winning are almost zero. You would bet your house that your ticket will lose. Yet you also believe that some ticket will win.
fields.dilemma: Is it rational to believe your ticket will lose while believing someone will win?
probes: Why do we buy tickets if we believe they will lose?
When is it okay to believe something that is mathematically unlikely?

reason: conversation 2, voice 2: The lottery paradox is an exercise in formal epistemology, sparking debate rather than dialogue.

fields.title: The Shadow Watchers
fields.setup: People have lived their entire lives chained in a cave facing a blank wall. Behind them is a fire. Things pass in front of the fire, casting shadows on the wall. The prisoners watch the shadows and give them names. For them, the shadows are the only reality. One prisoner is freed, goes outside, and sees the sun and real trees.
fields.dilemma: Can the freed prisoner ever explain the real world to those left in the cave?
probes: Would the prisoners think the freed person had gone crazy?
How do you know you are not watching shadows right now?

reason: judge: same as "The Shadows" (0.64)

fields.title: The Clean Slate
fields.setup: You have just read the greatest book you will ever read. The ending surprised you so completely that you gasped out loud. A doctor offers you a safe pill that will erase only the memory of reading this specific book. You will forget the plot, the characters, and the twist ending.
fields.dilemma: Do you take the pill so you can experience reading it for the first time again?
probes: Does a great experience lose its value if you keep wiping it away to start over?

reason: Engaging, whimsical premise with a poignant second probe about wiping relationship memories.

fields.title: The Garage Sale
fields.setup: You are at a neighborhood garage sale. You see an old watch sitting on a folding table with a $5 sticker. You happen to know vintage watches well. This specific model is a rare Rolex worth at least $10,000. The person running the sale is an older woman clearing out her late husband's things. She seems to be struggling for money.
fields.dilemma: Do you buy the watch for $5?
probes: What if the seller was a wealthy collector who just made a mistake?
What if the watch was only worth $200?
Do you have an obligation to tell strangers they are making a bad deal?

reason: A sharp, concrete test of transactional honesty against pure personal windfall.

fields.title: The Muddy Shoes
fields.setup: You are wearing brand new expensive shoes. You are walking past a shallow pond on your way to an important job interview. You see a small child thrashing in the water. There is no one else around. If you wade in to save the child, you will ruin your shoes and miss your interview, but you will easily save their life.
fields.dilemma: Do you wade into the pond?
probes: Would you judge someone who walked right past?

Does distance change your moral duty?

reason: another retelling of "Peter Singer, 1972" scored higher

fields.title: The Hidden Will
fields.setup: Your wealthy uncle passes away. While cleaning his study, you find a hidden handwritten will dated a week before his death. In it, he leaves his entire fortune to a controversial political group you deeply despise. The current legal will leaves everything to a struggling children's hospital. fields.dilemma: Do you destroy the handwritten will?
probes: Does a dead person have a right to control their money?
What if he left the money to your irresponsible sibling instead of a political group?
Are you willing to steal to fund a good cause?

reason: Juicy moral dilemma pitting dead-hand autonomy against active societal good and raw personal bias.

fields.title: The Blind Lottery
fields.setup: You are tasked with designing a brand new society from scratch. You get to decide the tax rates, the healthcare system, the laws, and how wealth is distributed. But there is a catch. You have to design it before you know who you will be in this society. You might be born rich, poor, healthy, disabled, gifted, or marginalized. You will be assigned your life completely at random.
fields.dilemma: Do you allow extreme wealth to exist in your new society?
probes: What is the highest risk you would take to potentially be a billionaire?
How poor are you willing to let the poorest person be?
Does gambling on your own success make you nervous?

reason: another retelling of "John Rawls, 1971" scored higher

fields.title: The Promotion
fields.setup: You and your coworker are up for the same promotion. You are both equally qualified. During a casual lunch, your coworker shares a brilliant idea for a new project. probes: What if your coworker stole an idea from you last year?

fields.title: The Banned Guest
fields.setup: You are planning your wedding. It is a small intimate event. Your oldest friend has been dating a partner who is completely toxic. fields.title: The Invisible Ring
fields.setup: You find a simple gold ring. When you put it on your finger and turn it, you become completely invisible. You can walk anywhere unseen. You can take whatever you want. You can listen to private conversations. You will never be caught. No one will ever know you have this power.

fields.title: The Delete Button
fields.setup: You are backing out of a parking spot and accidentally scrape the side of a beautiful sports car. It leaves a massive deep scratch. No one saw you do it. There are no cameras. fields.title: The Perfect Simulation
fields.setup: Scientists have invented a machine that can simulate any reality you want. If you plug into it, you will feel like you are writing a great novel, making friends, or falling in love. fields.title: The Novel
fields.setup: Your best friend has spent five years writing a novel. They quit their job and drained their savings to finish it. They finally hand you the manuscript and ask for your honest opinion. fields.title: The Drowning Child
fields.setup: You are wearing your best outfit. You walk past a shallow pond and see a child drowning. You can wade in and save them, but it will ruin your clothes. You would obviously save the child. Right now, that same amount of money could save a dying child on the other side of the world.

fields.title: The Dream Job

fields.title: The Experience Machine

fields.title: The Career Reset

fields.title: The Veil of Ignorance

fields.title: The Secret Saver

fields.title: The Last Conversation
